terms.grammar: adjective; the comparative is rare, and the superlative novissimus means “last”
terms.comment: Of anything not old or not used before: a new book, new shoes, a new teacher. “What’s new?” is Quid novī? (see what’s new?). The superlative is “last”: novissimum agmen, the rear of a column (Caes. BG 1.15, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: fresh, recent, just made or picked
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “that has not long existed”, as distinct from novus: fresh cheese, fresh figs, a recent wrong. A newborn is recēns nātus (see newborn).

phrases.latin: cui dōnō lepidum novum libellum āridā modo pūmice expolītum?
phrases.english: who shall I give my nice new little book to, just polished with dry pumice?

phrases.latin: cum recentī fīcō salis vice cāseō vescī nūper excōgitātum est
phrases.english: eating cheese with fresh figs, instead of salt, is a recent discovery
